client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. I keep getting hit with waves of sadness at random times during the workday - I'll see something that reminds me of her and suddenly I can't focus at all. I'm not sure talking about it will help because the pain just feels so raw and real, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're experiencing these waves of grief quite intensely, especially when unexpected reminders come up during your day. While you're saying the pain feels too raw to talk about, I notice your voice softens when you mention her - would you be willing to share what comes up when you think about your grandma now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I don't know...it's just that everything still feels so fresh, even though it's been months. When I think about her, I get this tightness in my chest remembering how she'd always have my favorite cookies waiting when I visited. But then I feel guilty because I didn't visit enough toward the end. 

I guess I'm afraid if I start talking about her, I'll just break down completely. And what's the point of that? She's gone and crying won't change anything.
therapist: The way you describe your grandma's cookies shows how much warmth and love was between you, even as you're wrestling with these painful feelings of guilt. You mention being afraid to break down - I wonder if part of you thinks you need to "hold it together" to honor her memory? What comes up when you imagine letting yourself feel this grief fully?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I never thought about it that way, but maybe you're right. The idea of really letting myself cry over Grandma makes me feel... I don't know, like I'd be disrespecting how strong she was. She never complained, even when she was sick. If I fall apart, it's like I'm not living up to her example. 

But at the same time, I do feel this heavy weight in my chest whenever I think about her. It's confusing because part of me wants to just sob, but another part thinks I should be able to handle this better by now.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two important truths at once - the deep love and admiration you have for your grandma's strength, and your own very human need to grieve. I notice you describe this so clearly even as your voice gets quieter - what would it mean to you if grieving fully could actually be another way of honoring her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I never thought about grief as a way to honor her... but that feels like a lot of pressure too. If I really let myself feel everything, I'm scared I'll just collapse into sadness and not be able to function. She was always so strong - wouldn't falling apart mean I'm failing her?
therapist: You're holding onto this idea that strength means not showing pain, just like your grandma did - but I wonder if there might be another kind of strength in allowing yourself to feel this loss fully? The way your voice catches when you talk about her suggests how much this relationship meant to you - what would it look like to grieve in a way that feels true to both your love for her and your own needs?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about different kinds of strength, but it's just... when I try to really feel the grief, it's like this tidal wave that might drown me. My grandma always said "tears don't fix anything," and part of me still believes that. 

What if I start crying and can't stop? I've seen people fall apart after losses and never really recover, and that terrifies me.
therapist: Your fear about being overwhelmed by grief comes through so clearly, especially when you describe it as a tidal wave. I notice though, as you share your grandma's words, your voice softens in a way that makes me wonder - might there be room to honor both her wisdom and your own emotional truth at the same time? What would it be like to experiment with small moments of allowing the tears, while still keeping your feet on solid ground?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

therapist: It sounds like your grandma's words about strength are still very present for you, even as your own emotions surface.
